extracted.intended_audience: researchers and teams planning or conducting scoping reviews (health professions / medical education researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, stepwise guidance for planning and carrying out a team-based scoping review: defining the question, searching and selecting studies, charting data, analyzing and reporting results, and (optionally) consulting stakeholders. Emphasis is on iterative methods, team roles, and quality-control procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and purpose of a scoping review
rubrics_metrics.description: A scoping review is a type of knowledge synthesis that uses a systematic and iterative approach to identify and synthesize an existing or emerging body of literature on a given topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main reasons: to map the extent, range, and nature of the literature and to determine possible gaps. Scoping reviews may include non–peer-reviewed literature and can precede other research or other review types (eg, systematic reviews).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying the research team (team composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scoping reviews are not conducted by a single individual; the team should include someone with content expertise and an individual with experience conducting scoping reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding a librarian who can assist with building the search strategy is extremely helpful. Thoughtful planning of team membership ensures the right knowledge, skills, and expertise to successfully complete the review and ensure findings contribute to the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulating the research question (scope and feasibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating the research question is a vital first step; the question should be neither too broad nor too narrow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A question that is too broad increases papers and may affect feasibility; too narrow may compromise breadth and depth. Conduct a preliminary literature search to determine: (1) breadth of the question; (2) whether a scoping review already exists; and (3) whether sufficient literature exists to warrant a scoping review. Consult a librarian to help decide if a scoping review is the appropriate method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early librarian consultation and search strategy construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Early consultation with a librarian should occur to build and refine the search strategy—keywords, Medical Subject Headings, and databases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refine strategy based on papers found; a librarian may confirm that there is insufficient literature or too much literature (necessitating a more targeted question). Use MeSH and controlled vocabulary where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining inclusion and exclusion criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Define clear inclusion and exclusion criteria aligned with the research question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss criteria with the research team to ensure diverse perspectives and alignment with the question. Refine criteria if searches return excessive 'noise' by identifying terms that introduce irrelevant papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of grey and non–peer-reviewed literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Scoping reviews are not limited to peer-reviewed literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider grey literature and other nontraditional sources as appropriate to fully map an evolving or emerging topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of screening and reference-management tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Use software (eg, Covidence, Rayyan) and reference-management tools (eg, EndNote) to organize citations and support screening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helpful features: import/export of citations, identification of duplicates, detecting similarity between abstracts, documentation of reasons for inclusion/exclusion, and blinding reviewers to each other's decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screening process and what to read
rubrics_metrics.description: Screening should include reading the title and the abstract; if an abstract is not available, conduct a full-text review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screening by title alone is insufficient because titles may not reflect paper contents accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer calibration and agreement thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Calibrate reviewers before full screening to ensure consistent application of criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A calibration exercise consists of selecting 5% to 10% of papers for independent screening by each reviewer. If agreement is low (eg, lower than 90%), discuss disagreements, review and possibly revise inclusion criteria, then run a second calibration (another ~10%). If two reviewers per paper is infeasible, one reviewer may screen with a second verifying a portion, aiming for 90% or better agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data charting (data extraction form development)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop the data extraction (charting) form collaboratively with the team, tailored to the research question and review purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common extraction categories: author, year, geographical location, study population, main results, study limitations, and future directions. More specific categories should be added as needed to capture data relevant to the question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilot testing and calibration of extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Pilot-test the extraction form and conduct calibration exercises to ensure consistency in charting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have dyads of reviewers independently extract data from a small number of papers (eg, 5–10), meet to discuss discrepancies, and refine the form if high agreement is not obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collating and presenting numerical results
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct numerical analyses on extracted data and present key findings to showcase salient aspects of the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present numerical findings in tables or charts. Ensure readers can see alignment between the presented findings and the objectives for conducting the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic analysis, coding, and development of themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform thematic analysis by examining text excerpts, creating codes, and iteratively developing a codebook that leads to categories and themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create tentative codes and modify them iteratively; review how codes relate to each other to identify patterns and form categories and themes. Reflexivity is essential—use memos to capture interpretive thoughts. The team should discuss clarity of operational definitions, how codes are named, and relationships among codes as codes are grouped into themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder consultation (optional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult stakeholders to obtain input on the research question, sources, interpretation of findings, and identification of gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholder consultation can be integrated at various stages (not only at the end) and can take the form of focus groups, individual interviews, or surveys. Purposes include refining questions/sources and shedding light on findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative flexibility of the scoping review process
rubrics_metrics.description: The methodological approach allows teams to move back to earlier stages as the review evolves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for and document iterations (eg, refining the research question, search strategy, inclusion criteria, or extraction items) as new insights arise during the review process.
